title: Methods
text:
Our workflow follows a structured parallel analysis of porcine and human transcriptomes:
Data Acquisition: Datasets were retrieved from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus: GSE61271 (Pig) and GSE162653 (Human).
Preprocessing: Human raw counts were processed using the DESeq2 vignette (Love et al., 2014). Pig data, provided as pre-normalized counts, was analyzed using the limma user guide (Ritchie et al., 2015).
Ortholog Mapping: Pig Ensembl IDs were converted to human gene symbols using biomaRt for cross-species compatibility.
Pathway Analysis: We employed GSVA to calculate enrichment scores for the MSigDB Hallmark Gene Set (Liberzon et al., 2015).

title: BNFO 420 - Capstone
text: In this study, there were limitations on several factors related to data availability and cross species comparison. The pig dataset (GSE6171) was already normalized and raw RNA-seq count was not available which prevented the ability to use standardized differential expression tools such as DESq2. A different approach was used, using limma for differential analysis. In contrast, the human dataset (GSE162653) contained raw counts, therefore this led to methodological inconsistency between analysis for both species and cross species. Additionally, the cross species gene mapping from pig to human orthologs may have resulted in incomplete gene matches which can potentially affect comparisons. The PCA analysis showed weak clustering by adiposity in pigs which suggests lower gene expression. Lastly, the analysis is based on transcriptomic data. Therefore, its correlation and cannot determine casualty between gene expression changes and obesity progressions.

title: BNFO 420 - Capstone
text:
2 Future Work

Future research will utilize single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq), specifically targeting the Bama pig atlas (Chen et al., 2025), to differentiate between adipocyte-specific and macrophage-specific inflammatory signals. We could also plan on conducting a depot-specific comparison (visceral vs. subcutaneous fat) to determine if the metabolic divergence observed is consistent across different adipose locations.

title: Pig vs Human Genome Comparison
text:
Obesity is a complex metabolic disorder characterized by excessive adipose tissue accumulation that extends beyond simple energy storage to include critical endocrine functions, such as the secretion of leptin to regulate appetite and systemic metabolism. The progression from leanness to obesity involves dynamic changes in fat cell size (hypertrophy), cell number (hyperplasia), and inflammatory status, all orchestrated by specific gene expression patterns. While human studies are essential, they are often confounded by lifestyle and genetic heterogeneity, making porcine (Sus scrofa) models an ideal translational alternative due to their remarkable metabolic and physiological similarities to humans.
In this study, we utilized two primary transcriptomic datasets: GSE61271 (RNA-sequencing of 36 pigs categorized by biological state: low, mean, and high weight) and GSE162653 (RNA-sequencing of 40 human white adipose tissue samples from normal-weight and obese individuals). Our primary objective was to perform a side-by-side comparative analysis of these datasets to determine if the directionality and magnitude of gene expression in the Leptin (LEP) pathway and associated inflammatory markers are conserved across species.
Our pipeline integrated DESeq2 for human raw count analysis and limma for normalized pig data, with cross-species ortholog mapping performed via biomaRt. While individual gene-level results showed significant divergence—with humans exhibiting 108 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) compared to only 4 in pigs—pathway-level analysis via Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) revealed striking conservation. Both species showed significant upregulation in inflammatory and immune pathways, specifically the Complement System and PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling. However, a significant metabolic divergence was observed: metabolism-related pathways were upregulated in pigs but downregulated in humans. These findings suggest that while the inflammatory hallmark of obesity is highly conserved, the metabolic response may differ based on the timeline of obesity progression or evolutionary adaptations. This research highlights the utility and the limitations of the porcine model in translational metabolic studies.

title: Pig vs Human Genome Comparison
text:
2 Background and Motivation

Obesity has reached pandemic proportions, dramatically increasing the risk of chronic comorbidities such as Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and hypertension (Manna & Jain, 2015). Adipose tissue is a dynamic endocrine organ that maintains homeostasis by secreting adipokines, most notably Leptin (LEP), which signals energy availability to the brain (Lu et al., 2015). In the obese state, this tissue undergoes profound remodeling characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress (Manna & Jain, 2015).

title: Pig vs Human Genome Comparison
text:
3 Rationale

Understanding the genetic drivers of obesity progression is difficult in humans due to uncontrolled environmental variables. Pigs serve as premier translational models because their fat deposition and metabolic syndrome progression closely mirror human biology (Spurlock & Gabler, 2008; Litten-Brown et al., 2010). However, it is critical to identify which specific molecular pathways are truly orthologous to ensure results from porcine studies can be accurately applied to human clinical targets.

title: Pig vs Human Genome Comparison
text:
4 Hypothesis

H₀ (Null): Adiposity status has no significant effect on the expression of the LEP pathway or inflammatory signaling in either pigs or humans.
H₁ (Alternate): Increasing adiposity levels will trigger a concordant upregulation of LEP and functionally co-expressed genes (RETN, FABP4, PLIN1, CFD, NAMPT, SERPINE1, SOCS3) and a significant increase in inflammatory pathway activity in both species.

title: Results
text:
2.1 Pig Obesity PCA






Figure analysis: Principal component analysis shows individual pig samples colored by obesity level. PCA was performed using the top 500 most variable genes from normalized RNA-seq counts. The three obesity groups show noticeable overlap, suggesting the pig dataset may not strongly separate by obesity level alone. However, it is still useful because it includes low, mean, and high adiposity groups, allowing obesity progression to be examined.

title: Results
text:
2.2 Pig Differential Expression Volcano Plot

Figure analysis: This volcano plot compares gene expression between high-weight and low-weight pigs. Red points represent significantly differentially expressed genes based on the chosen p-value and log2 fold-change thresholds. The small number of significant genes suggests that obesity-related gene expression differences in pigs may be more subtle compared to humans.

title: Results
text:
2.3 Pig Hypothesis-Driven Gene Trend Correlation






Figure analysis: A bar graph was used to assess how selected adiposity-related genes correlate with increasing adiposity. Each bar represents the Spearman correlation for a gene, indicating whether expression increases, decreases, or shows no clear trend. Of the hypothesized genes, four (PLIN1, CFD, NAMPT, SERPINE1) were present. Notably, NAMPT and SERPINE1 showed positive correlations above 0.3, indicating increased expression with higher adiposity, while the others showed weaker or inconsistent trends. Overall, the results partially support the hypothesis, suggesting gene-specific rather than uniform expression changes.

title: Results
section: 2.4 Pig Top 30 Most Variable Genes Heatmap
text:
2.4 Pig Top 30 Most Variable Genes Heatmap






Figure analysis: This heatmap shows an unbiased analysis of overall gene expression was conducted using the top 30 most variable genes across adiposity levels. The heatmap shows clear differences between low and high adiposity groups, reflected by distinct blue (low expression) and red (high expression) patterns. This suggests a proportional relationship between adiposity and gene expression for certain genes. The accompanying dendrogram groups genes with similar expression patterns, indicating potential co-regulated gene clusters that may be involved in shared biological processes such as immune response, inflammation, and oxygen transport.

title: Results
text:
2.5 Pig Heatmaps by Biological State

LowMeanHigh



























Figure analysis: To further investigate gene expression changes, the data were separated by biological state (low, mean, high adiposity) while keeping the same set of top genes for comparison. Although the heatmaps may initially appear inconsistent, they reflect the same genes across different adiposity groups. Closer examination shows that genes such as PCK1, TREH, LYZ, SPP1, CSF3R, PADI2, MSR1, and DDX60 increase in expression together as adiposity rises, suggesting coordinated involvement in metabolic and inflammatory processes. At the same time, other genes decrease in expression, indicating that adiposity is associated with both upregulation and downregulation of different biological pathways.
